messages.subject: simmer problem definition (de)serializer
messages.body_plain:
Over time simmer has become a more and more mature DES framework (much thanks to Iñaki).

I currently use simmer mostly in an ad-hoc analysis kind of way: simulating a current system and formulating an advise on it. However, I would like to start using it in a more dynamic way, e.g. integrating it into a website front-end or in existing IT systems. To easily achieve this I think a (de)serializer is the way to go. Another advantage is also that it will become easy to share problem definitions (e.g. for educational purposes).

I'm currently thinking of defining the problem definition in a JSON structure.

Here are two examples: https://gist.github.com/Bart6114/0924637a5cf823e54c360c0f54504731 and https://gist.github.com/Bart6114/08bee48bd9e57639aa5ab889a9f8d2c8. The first one is a simple example, the second one contains a more complex branching trajectory. A value encapsulated with "%" will be transformed to a function (if it doesn't evaluate to a function). A value encapsulated with "$" will be evaluated as R code.

I currently have some code up and running for deserialisation (I'll put it up on GitHub), but not yet for serialisation; will have to look into whether every required can be easily accessed.

What do you guys think about the proposed JSON structure? Any other ideas about the (de)serialization?

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] simmer problem definition (de)serializer
messages.body_plain:
It would be a nice feature indeed. Deserialisation is more or less straightforward, and your proposed JSON structure seems natural to me and easy to use. We may find some clues on this issue in the jsonlite <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/jsonlite/index.html> and RJSONIO <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/RJSONIO/index.html> packages.

The problem comes with serialisation of certain arguments. For instance, once you’ve called at(0, 0, 0), you lose the information about the caller and (which is more important) about the values, and all you have is the returned function, which is:
> at(0,0,0)
function() {
    if (i < length(time_diffs)) {
      i <<- i+1
      return(time_diffs[i])
    } else {
      return(-1)
    }
  }
<environment: 0x3eaadc8>

As you can see, the values are masked into the time_diffs variable. :-\

Iñaki
​

messages.subject: How to branch based on which of 2 generators an entity comes from
messages.subject_clean: How to branch based on which of 2 generators an entity comes from
messages.body_plain:
Hi friends,

I'd like to have two generators (with different probability functions), whose entities go through the same trajectory but branch based on which generator they come from.  I am not sure how to access this info (i.e. which method to use) at the branch point about which gen they came from - in the example they are dogs or cats.   Basic code below, which needs the branch decision function to be modified.  Please let me know if any of this does not make sense.

Thanks & Cheers,

Lindsay

###########

t0 <- create_trajectory("my trajectory") %>%
        seize("receptionist", 1) %>% #Both dogs and cats go to the receptionist
        timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,5,2))) %>%
        release("receptionist", 1) %>%
        ##Here is where I want to branch depending on what generator made the entity
        branch(function() sample(1:2, 1), merge=c(TRUE, TRUE), ##Replace 'sample()' with a new function
                create_trajectory("cats") %>%
                        seize("catDoc", 1) %>%
                        timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
                        release("catDoc", 1),
                create_trajectory("cats") %>%
                        seize("dogDoc", 1) %>%
                        timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
                        release("dogDoc", 1)
       )

env <- simmer("Lab6") %>%
        add_resource("receptionist", 1) %>%
        add_resource("catDoc", 1) %>%
        add_resource("dogDoc", 1) %>%
        add_generator("cat", t0, function() rexp(1,rate = (1/45)), mon = 2) %>%
        add_generator("dog", t0, function() rexp(1,rate = (1/30)), mon = 2) %>%
        run(until=720) #720 = 12 hours * 60 min

--
“The time will come when diligent research over long periods will bring to light things which now lie hidden."

Seneca the Younger

Hi Lindsay,

The whole point behind the concept of trajectory is being a common path for arrivals of the same type. If you have two types of arrivals, cats and dogs, the natural way to model this problem with simmer is having two distinct trajectories, because they do different things even though they share some activities.   seize("receptionist", 1) %>% #Both dogs and cats go to the receptionist

  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,5,2))) %>%
  release("receptionist", 1

) %>%
  seize("catDoc", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
  release("catDoc", 1)

t.dog <- create_trajectory("dog") %>%
  seize("receptionist", 1) %>% #Both dogs and cats go to the receptionist

  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,5,2))) %>%
  release("receptionist", 1

) %>%
  seize("dogDoc", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
  release("dogDoc", 1)

env <- simmer("Lab6") %>%
  add_resource("receptionist", 1) %>%
  add_resource("catDoc", 1) %>%
  add_resource("dogDoc", 1) %>%
  add_generator("cat", t.cat <http://t.cat>, function() rexp(1,rate = (1/45)), mon = 2) %>%

  run(until=720) #720 = 12 hours * 60 min

Regards,
Iñaki

I think the previous email answered the question. But, as a side discussion, certainly it would be nice not to have to repeat the common activities in each trajectory. So I’ll examine the possibility of adding trajectories, of trajectory concatenation, as a future feature. This way, we could define
t.common <- create_trajectory("common") %>%
  seize("receptionist", 1) %>% #Both dogs and cats go to the receptionist

  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,5,2))) %>%
  release("receptionist", 1)

t.cat <http://t.cat> <- create_trajectory("cat"

) %>%
  seize("catDoc", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
  release("catDoc", 1)

t.dog <- create_trajectory("dog") %>%
  seize("dogDoc", 1) %>%
  timeout(function() max(0,rnorm(1,30,10))) %>%
  release("dogDoc", 1)

And then, we could simply concatenate them (tentative syntax follows):
env %>%
  add_generator("cat", t.common + t.cat <http://t.cat>, function() rexp(1,rate = (1/45)), mon = 2) %>%
  add_generator("dog", t.common + t.dog, function() rexp(1,rate = (1/30)), mon = 2)

Opinions welcome!

Regards,
Iñaki

messages.body_plain:
I am modeling a customer service operation with 10 agents (add_resource("engineer", 10, Inf))handling a stream of tickets. New tickets are assigned to any available agent. 40% of the time that agent can resolve and close the ticket. In the other 60% the agent must request additional information from the customer and wait for that customer to respond. When the customer responds, the ticket becomes active again and must go back to the same agent.

In the trajectory below I think any available agent would be assigned the ticket.

How would I go about seizing a particular agent? Could this be handled using attributes?

cases <-

  create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%

    seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%

  branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),

    create_trajectory("first day close") %>%

  # agent can close this case

      timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60)) %>%

      release("engineer", amount = 1.0),

    create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%

  # agent does research but will need more information from customer

  # do the research and send customer the request for information

      timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333)) %>%

      release("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%

  # now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond

      timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

  # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed

  # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

      seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%

      rollback("research/analyze", amount = 1, function()sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))

) %>%

  release("engineer", amount = 1.0)

The last release will be never executed because you set merge=c(F, F), and you don’t need it, because you release the engineer inside the branch. So it can be removed.
The rollback syntax is not correct. The correct one would be the following:

The rollback activity can climb up levels, so you can go back to the very first seize without repeating it inside the branch. That first seize is 4 hops away, so

cases <- create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%
  seize("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%
  branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),
         create_trajectory("first day close") %>%
           # agent can close this case
           timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60)) %>%
           release("engineer", amount = 1.0),

         create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%
           # agent does research but will need more information from customer
           # do the research and send customer the request for information
           timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333)) %>%
           release("engineer", amount = 1.0) %>%
           # now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond
           timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

           # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed
           # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

           rollback(amount = 4, function() sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))
  )

And now, straight to the point: no, it’s not possible to seize a particular agent right now. But it’s an interesting problem. I need to think deeper about it. The first question is: is it statistically significant? I mean, seizing the same or not. Maybe it is, but it’s not clear to me. Let me think about it.

messages.body_plain:
You have a point there, Lindsay. Indeed, if tickets must go back to the same agent, it means that agents are distinguisable, so they must be different resources with their own queues. But the model grows linearly with the number of engineers. First of all, you’ll need one trajectory per engineer:
engineers <- sapply(1:10, function(i) {
  name <- paste0("engineer", i)
  traj <- create_trajectory("Resolve new Case") %>%
    seize(name, amount = 1.0) %>%
    branch(function() sample(1:2, 1, FALSE, c(0.4, 0.6)), merge = c(F, F),
           create_trajectory("first day close") %>%

# agent can close this case
             timeout(function() runif(1, 30, 60

)) %>%
             release(name, amount = 1.0),

           create_trajectory("research/analyze") %>%

# agent does research but will need more information from customer
             # do the research and send customer the request for information
             timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.0333

)) %>%
             release(name, amount = 1.0) %>%

# now engineer is now free but case is not yet resolved - wait for customer to respond
             timeout(function() rexp(1, 0.1666) ) %>%

             # repeat this cycle of steps a random number of times until the case is closed
             # roll back this trajectory and repeat with probability 30%

             rollback(amount = 4, check = function() sample(0:1, 1, FALSE, c(0.3, 0.7)))
    )
  result <- list()
  result[[name]] <- traj
  result
})

Then, you need a function to check all engineers and select the one with less tickets:
selector <- function() {
  which.min(sapply(1:length(engineers), function(i) {
    env %>% get_server_count(names(engineers)[i]) +
      env %>% get_queue_count(names(engineers)[i])
  }))
}

And finally, you need to put everything inside a branch governed by the selector above:
case <- create_trajectory("select engineer")
do.call(branch, c(list(case, selector, merge=rep(F, 10)), engineers))

And of course, you’ll want to add the resources to the simulation environment:
env <- simmer()
for (i in names(engineers)) add_resource(env, i, 1, Inf)

Nice one, uh? ;-)

Thanks for the ideas. The reason the ticket must go back to the original engineer is because that engineer has developed experience working the problem to that point. Starting over with a new engineer can frustrate customers as he/she may repeat the same questions already asked by engineer 1 (“what release are you running?”, “do you have fix xxx applied?”, etc.)

I will try modeling using a different resource for each engineer, perhaps starting with a team of 2 engineers.

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Seize a specific resource
messages.body_plain:
Yeap, I understand the real scenario. What is not clear to me is that returning to the very same agent in the model, in the simulation, makes a real difference. Because in the simulation you have more flexibility, and you can, for instance, reduce the average research time for each rollback performed, thus simulating the experience gained.

If all your variables have the memoryless property (that is, exponential service times), then the identity of the agent is probably irrelevant. But this is only an educated guess. You can test both possibilities.

I've been fondling the idea of building a small web interface on top of simmer for demonstration purposes.
What it boils down to however is the difficulty of talking from a language/framework/tool to R and in turn to simmer. There are some adhoc solutions (think of e.g. rpy2), but they are IMO quite adhoc and I try to refrain from using them in production. A "package" that translate a JSON object (something that can be easily constructed in almost every language) into a ready-to-go simmer environment could be useful for these purposes.

To make it a bit more concrete: for the small web interface I'm talking about I would e.g. build the front-end using AngularJS, create a small HTTP backend in R using jug (https://github.com/Bart6114/jug - heavily biased here :) ) which can work with the simmer.json package. In the front-end you can then construct a problem definition in a visual way, the AngularJS controller translates it into a JSON object, does a POST request using the definition object, the jug instance receives the JSON and calls simmer.json::deserialise(JSON), runs the simulation and returns the result.

messages.subject: Re: [simmer-devel] Re: Big O and Simmer?
messages.body_plain:

The complexity of a model emerges from the number of steps that the underlying algorithm requires. Ok, thanks, I see. Several things here:

env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <- conf # Change global conf
  env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
  get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
}

That wrap() above is useless there, because 1) you are not assigning the result to any variable (wrapped <- env %>% ... %>% wrap()) and 2) you don’t really need it in this case.
The line input <- conf is NOT changing the global variable input. You are creating a local one with the same name, and the trajectory, as it is defined in a parent scope, uses the parent input, not that one. If you want to change the global input, you need to do input <<- conf. Note the double arrow assignment operator.
The reset() function is not resetting the generator function, so at(...) generates its 10 arrivals in the first run and that’s it. This is a bug and that’s why you are not getting results in the second run. Thank you, I’ll open an issue and I’ll fix it in the next release. ;-)

In the meantime, the hack #2 should work well. In fact, it’s not a hack at all. I mean, it’s just fine to define a new environment for each new simulation. It’s a hard reset. But in order to be able to use now() inside a trajectory defined in a parent scope, again, you need to use the double arrow assignment:

run_sim <- function(conf)
{
  input <<- conf # Change global conf

  # Redefine the parent environment. This should not complain about anything

  env <<- simmer("Global Env for now() to work"

)
  env %>%
    add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2) %>%
    add_resource("life", Inf, 0) %>%
    run(36500) %>% # useless wrap() removed
    get_mon_arrivals(per_resource = T)
}

run_sim(TRUE)

run_sim(FALSE)

If you don’t want global variables at all, then you can define the trajectory inside run_sim() and switch back to single arrow assignments.

As far as I know, <- never assigns to globals in any circumstances. From the help (? assignOps):
>
> The operators <- and = assign into the environment in which they are evaluated. The operator <- can be used anywhere, whereas the operator = is only allowed at the top level (e.g., in the complete expression typed at the command prompt) or as one of the subexpressions in a braced list of expressions.
>
> The operators <<- and ->> are normally only used in functions, and cause a search to be made through parent environments for an existing definition of the variable being assigned. If such a variable is found (and its binding is not locked) then its value is redefined, otherwise assignment takes place in the global environment.

messages.body_plain:
Ah, yes. I got confused because it will pull from a global.

On Fri, May 20, 2016 at 10:55 AM, Iñaki Úcar <i.uc...@gmail.com> wrote:

> As far as I know, <- never assigns to globals in any circumstances. From the help (? assignOps):
> >
> > The operators <- and = assign into the environment in which they are evaluated. The operator <- can be used anywhere, whereas the operator = is only allowed at the top level (e.g., in the complete expression typed at the command prompt) or as one of the subexpressions in a braced list of expressions.
> >
> > The operators <<- and ->> are normally only used in functions, and cause a search to be made through parent environments for an existing definition of the variable being assigned. If such a variable is found (and its binding is not locked) then its value is redefined, otherwise assignment takes place in the global environment.
> ​
>
> 2016-05-20 16:38 GMT+02:00 Shawn Garbett <shawn....@gmail.com>:
> > Wow, works like a charm. The <<- and <- I understand, but the <- assigns to globals in some circumstances. However, it's far better to be explicit.
> >
> > On Fri, May 20, 2016 at 7:48 AM, Iñaki Úcar <i.uc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > >
> > > Ok, thanks, I see. Several things here:
> > > env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
> > >
> > > run_sim <- function(conf)
> > > {
> > >   input <- conf # Change global conf
> > >   env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
> > >   get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
> > > }
> > > That wrap() above is useless there, because 1) you are not assigning the result to any variable (wrapped <- env %>% ... %>% wrap()) and 2) you don’t really need it in this case.
> > > The line input <- conf is NOT changing the global variable input. You are creating a local one with the same name, and the trajectory, as it is defined in a parent scope, uses the parent input, not that one. If you want to change the global input, you need to do input <<- conf. Note the double arrow assignment operator.
> > > The reset() function is not resetting the generator function, so at(...) generates its 10 arrivals in the first run and that’s it. This is a bug and that’s why you are not getting results in the second run. Thank you, I’ll open an issue and I’ll fix it in the next release. ;-)
> > >
> > > In the meantime, the hack #2 should work well. In fact, it’s not a hack at all. I mean, it’s just fine to define a new environment for each new simulation. It’s a hard reset. But in order to be able to use now() inside a trajectory defined in a parent scope, again, you need to use the double arrow assignment:
> > > run_sim <- function(conf)
> > > {
> > >   input <<- conf # Change global conf
> > >
> > >   # Redefine the parent environment. This should not complain about anything
> > >   env <<- simmer("Global Env for now() to work")
> > >   env %>%
> > >     add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2) %>%
> > >     add_resource("life", Inf, 0) %>%
> > >     run(36500) %>% # useless wrap() removed
> > >     get_mon_arrivals(per_resource = T)
> > > }
> > >
> > > run_sim(TRUE)
> > >
> > > run_sim(FALSE)
> > >
> > > If you don’t want global variables at all, then you can define the trajectory inside run_sim() and switch back to single arrow assignments.
> > > ​
> > >
> > > 2016-05-19 22:04 GMT+02:00 Shawn Garbett <shawn....@gmail.com>:
> > > > I don't have a fully working example, but here goes my best attempt at showing what I'm working on:
> > > >
> > > > library(simmer)
> > > >
> > > > env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # Not used in this example, but main code needs this
> > > >
> > > > # Configuration for model run, will be called from another R package with this info
> > > > # Doing this as a global
> > > > input <- TRUE
> > > >
> > > > # Create some resources
> > > > env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)
> > > >
> > > > # May terminate
> > > > event <- function(traj)
> > > > {
> > > >   traj %>% branch(
> > > >     function() sample(1:2, 1, prob=c(0.8,0.2)),
> > > >     merge=c(TRUE,FALSE),
> > > >     create_trajectory() %>% timeout(1), # Something non-fatal happened
> > > >     create_trajectory() %>% release("life")
> > > >   )
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > traj <- create_trajectory() %>%
> > > >         seize("life") %>%
> > > >         branch(function() input+1,
> > > >                merge=c(FALSE,TRUE),
> > > >                create_trajectory() %>%
> > > >                  timeout(40) %>%
> > > >                  release("life"),
> > > >                create_trajectory() %>%
> > > >                  event()
> > > >         ) %>%
> > > >         rollback(amount=1, times=100)
> > > >
> > > > env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
> > > >
> > > > run_sim <- function(conf)
> > > > {
> > > >   input <- conf # Change global conf
> > > >   env %>% reset() %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
> > > >   get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > run_sim(TRUE)
> > > >
> > > > run_sim(FALSE) # NO OUTPUT!!!!, doesn't matter if configuration is flipped, the 2nd run is empty
> > > >
> > > > # Well that didn't work, now for hacked permutative guessing
> > > > run_sim <- function(conf)
> > > > {
> > > >   input <- conf # Change global conf
> > > >
> > > >   env %>% reset()
> > > >   env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
> > > >   env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
> > > >   get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > run_sim(TRUE) # Still no output, probably didn't need to add generator
> > > >
> > > > # Hack #2, Seems to work--but does weird things in a larger simulation around resources.
> > > > run_sim <- function(conf)
> > > > {
> > > >   input <- conf # Change global conf
> > > >
> > > >   # Blow global environment away!!!
> > > >   env <- simmer("Global Env for now() to work") # And it complains that it already is defined
> > > >   env %>% add_generator("patient", traj, at(rep(0, 10)), mon=2)
> > > >   env %>% add_resource("life", Inf, 0)
> > > >   env %>% run(36500) %>% wrap()
> > > >   get_mon_arrivals(env, per_resource = T)
> > > > }
> > > >
> > > > run_sim(TRUE)
> > > >
> > > > run_sim(FALSE)
> > > >
> > > > Hack #2 appears to work in this example, but at the expense of blowing away the environment. However, in my larger code base, the first model run works great. Then in the Hack #2 run, it doesn't always release resources, even when run with the same input!
> > > >
> > > > On Thu, May 19, 2016 at 1:49 PM, Iñaki Úcar <i.uc...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > > > I don't understand the problem. Could you provide us with a brief example, please?
> > > > >
> > > > > 2016-05-19 20:36 GMT+02:00 Shawn Garbett <shawn....@gmail.com>:
> > > > > > This is proving to be a problem for me. 'env' as a global variable is now forcing my model inputs to be a global as well.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > I have a list of "inputs". These control trajectory behavior through permutations to compare. So, I wrote a function where the patient trajectory is a function of inputs. Now, if I reset the global env, the generator's that were added are still present. The only solution is to now make inputs a global variable as well, since I can't way to delete a previously defined generator.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > So, now 'env' and 'inputs' are now forced to be global objects. I prefer a more functional approach that doesn't depend on environment globals.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > The best solution to all this is if there was a 'now()' function that worked in a trajectory and it didn't depend on accessing a global variable.
